DNA polymerase III is the principal DNA polymerase in chromosomal DNA replication as it is responsible for the synthesis of the new DNA strand. It is also known as the replicative polymerase and is highly processive, meaning it can add many nucleotides without dissociating from the DNA template. It requires a free 3'-hydroxyl group on a primer to add the next nucleotide (forming a phosphodiester bond with the 5'-phosphate of the incoming dNTP). It is not efficient at nick translation (the process of filling in the gaps in the lagging strand) but rather DNA polymerase I is responsible for this. It is not the most abundant DNA polymerase in E. coli as DNA polymerase I is more abundant. It cannot initiate replication without a primer as it can only add nucleotides to an existing 3'-hydroxyl group.

DNA polymerase III catalyses the synthesis of the new DNA strand and is most likely to occur at sites rich in (A-T) base pairs as these are easier to separate as they are held together by only two hydrogen bonds.

Without NAD+, glycolysis cannot proceed and thus no ATP can be produced.Lactate is not produced to prevent further strain on the muscles as it is only produced when exercising, as it is not a mechanism of defense against further strain on the muscles. It does not cause pain in the area because of its acidic profile, thus it does not conserve muscle integrity by preventing further exercise.Instead, lactate is produced to prevent cell lysis. Pyruvate cannot be converted into acetyl-CoA in the absence of oxygen as the process requires an oxygen molecule. Unlike lactate, pyruvic acid can be transported to the liver to be converted to glucose, so its build-up can be lethal to the cell.
